summary: Specifies how to carry IPv6 over DECT Ultra Low Energy, a low-power wireless technology from cordless telephony.

plainLanguage.summary: Lets little cordless-phone radios carry internet traffic for small gadgets.

questions: how does ipv6 work over dect ule
what mtu does ipv6 over dect ule use
how is the interface identifier derived in dect ule
subtitle: How tiny battery-powered DECT cordless-phone radios carry IPv6 traffic using 6LoWPAN tricks.

tldr.problem: DECT Ultra Low Energy (ULE) radios power sensors, meters and home-automation devices, and those devices want IPv6 without wasting scarce battery on protocol overhead.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adapts the 6LoWPAN toolbox (header compression, optimized Neighbor Discovery, link-local addressing) to the DECT ULE star topology, sets the link MTU to 1280 octets so no fragmentation layer is needed, and derives interface identifiers from DECT device addresses.
tldr.outcome: DECT ULE nodes can be ordinary IPv6 hosts behind a gateway that acts as the 6LoWPAN Border Router. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Identities
facts.value: IPEI and RFPI 40 bits, TPUI 20 bits

today: RFC 8105 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification for IPv6 over DECT ULE; the text itself builds on the 6LoWPAN specifications RFC 4944, RFC 6282 and RFC 6775.

sections.title: Why IPv6 over DECT ULE
sections.content:
DECT (Digital Enhanced Cordless Telecommunications) is an ETSI standard series. DECT ULE (Ultra Low Energy) builds on it but cuts power consumption sharply at the expense of data throughput. The RFC gives two example uses: a home-security sensor that sends a few bytes at periodic intervals but can wake on an event such as a break-in, and a pendant for the elderly that sends periodic status messages and can open a voice connection in an emergency.

The RFC argues for IPv6 on these devices because of its large address space and well-known infrastructure. DECT ULE resembles IEEE 802.15.4, so a subset of the mechanisms from RFC 4944, RFC 6282 and RFC 6775 can be reused. The mapping is also inspired by RFC 7668 (IPv6 over Bluetooth Low Energy).
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny gadgets in your home want to join the internet, but they run on small batteries. This RFC borrows tricks from other small-gadget networks so they can.

sections.title: The DECT ULE Stack and Roles
sections.content:
The DECT ULE physical layer works in the 1880 - 1920 MHz band, depending on region, at a symbol rate of 1.152 Mbaud. The Data Link Control (DLC) layer provides multiplexing plus segmentation and reassembly, applies per-message authentication and encryption, preserves packet order and integrity, and delivers on a best-effort basis.

Two roles matter. The Portable Part (PP) is the power-constrained device, typically a sensor, and acts as a 6LoWPAN node (6LN). The Fixed Part (FP) is the gateway or base station and acts as the 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR). The RFC covers only this primary scenario; other role combinations are out of scope.

Applications use a Permanent Virtual Circuit (PVC) over the ULE stack. The application protocol is negotiated when the PVC is set up, and the identifier for 6LoWPAN is 0x06. Only the packet-mode data service is addressed; the DECT ULE MAC broadcast service is not used for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of devices. The little battery sensor is like a kid with a walkie-talkie, and the gateway is like the parent who is always plugged in and passes messages along.

sections.title: Star Topology and Subnets
sections.content:
At the link layer, communication happens only between an FP and a PP, and one FP can handle many PPs at once. So a radio hop is equivalent to an IPv6 link. Unlike IEEE 802.15.4, DECT ULE in its primary configuration does not form multihop networks, so the mesh header from RFC 4944 MUST NOT be used and the 6LoWPAN Router (6LR) role is not defined. DECT ULE repeaters work transparently and are out of scope.

Because each PP has its own link to the FP, PPs cannot hear each other. The RFC therefore chooses a Multi-Link Subnet model (see RFC 4903), specifically non-broadcast multi-access (NBMA) at Layer 2. The whole DECT ULE network can be one subnet using one /64 prefix, with the 6LBR forwarding packets from one 6LN to another. Link-local multicast reaches only a single DECT ULE connection, so 6LN-to-6LN traffic with link-local addresses is impossible.

The RFC describes three scenarios: a network connected to the Internet, an isolated network (where the FP numbers the network with a ULA prefix per RFC 4193 and routes between PPs), and several FPs, each a wireless cell, sharing one /64 prefix with the FPs behaving as Backbone Routers (6BBR).
sections.plainLanguage: Every sensor can only talk to the gateway, never straight to another sensor, like kids who can only pass notes through the teacher. The gateway passes each note on.

sections.title: Addresses and Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
Each PP gets an IPEI (40 bits) at manufacture, and each FP gets an RFPI (also 40 bits). During location registration the FP assigns a 20-bit TPUI to the PP for Layer 2 addressing, but because many implementations keep reusing the same TPUI it is not suitable for building the interface identifier (see RFC 8065).

Both 6LN and 6LBR MUST create a link-local address from their DECT device address. The IPEI (for a 6LN) or RFPI (for a 6LBR) is expanded with leading zero bits to 48 bits. The most significant bit is set to one for RFPI-derived addresses and to zero for IPEI-derived ones. The 64-bit IID is then derived following Appendix A of RFC 4291. The U/L bit stays zero, marking the IID as not globally unique, which is fine because link-local addresses must never leave the subnet.

For non-link-local addresses, a 6LN SHOULD NOT use IIDs derived from a MAC-48 or DECT device address. Cryptographically Generated Addresses, privacy extensions, Hash-Based Addresses, DHCPv6 or static semantically opaque addresses SHOULD be used by default. If an IID is not globally unique, Duplicate Address Detection MUST be used. The 6LBR gets its prefix by means outside this RFC, for example DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation or a ULA, and MUST set the on-link (L) flag to zero in the Prefix Information Option, so 6LNs always send packets via the 6LBR.
sections.plainLanguage: Each gadget already has a serial number from the factory. The gateway turns that number into a home address, and for addresses used out on the wider internet it picks hard-to-guess ones so nobody can track the gadget.

sections.title: MTU, Fragmentation and Multicast
sections.content:
A single DECT ULE MAC packet holds 38 octets, enough for small periodic readings. IPv6 packets can be much bigger, but the DLC layer natively segments and reassembles any MTU below 65536 octets. The DECT ULE default MTU is 500 octets; this specification says the DLC layer SHALL be configured with an MTU of 1280 octets. As a result, the fragmentation and reassembly of RFC 4944 MUST NOT be used.

Larger packets cost battery life, because the stack splits them into many MAC packets and each one consumes power to send or receive.

The MAC layer broadcast service cannot carry IPv6-sized packets, so traffic is always unicast between two nodes. To send a multicast to all its 6LNs, the 6LBR must copy the packet and unicast it on each link, which may not be energy efficient (take particular care if the FP is battery-powered). The 6LBR MUST track multicast listeners per link and MUST NOT forward multicast packets to 6LNs that have not registered for the group. A 6LN that wants to send multicast unicasts it to the 6LBR, which forwards it.
sections.plainLanguage: Big messages get cut into small pieces by the radio itself. Each piece uses a little battery, so small messages are best. To tell everyone something, the gateway has to whisper to each gadget one by one.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery on the Link
sections.content:
Once the DECT ULE link is up, address configuration can begin. A PP sets up a service call and specifies the <<IWU-ATTRIBUTES>> with the application protocol identifier 0x06 and an MTU of 1280 octets or larger. The FP replies with a service-change-accept that MUST contain a valid paging descriptor, and the PP MUST listen for paging messages as described there. Then IPv6 packets can flow.

After forming its link-local address and joining the all-nodes multicast address, the 6LN sends Router Solicitations as in RFC 4861 and RFC 6775. Only the parts of the RFC 6775 optimizations that suit a star topology apply. A 6LN MUST NOT register its link-local address, because the IID maps uniquely to its Layer 2 address. It MUST register every non-link-local address with the 6LBR by sending a Neighbor Solicitation with an Address Registration Option (ARO), whatever method generated the IID, and process the Neighbor Advertisement in reply.
sections.plainLanguage: When a gadget wakes up, it knocks on the gateway's door and asks how to join. If it picks a new address for outside use, it tells the gateway so mail finds it.

sections.title: Header Compression
sections.content:
All headers MUST be compressed using the RFC 6282 formats. The IPv6 payload length is derived from the DLC packet length, and elided addresses are rebuilt from the Layer 2 address.

For link-local traffic, both source and destination addresses MUST be elided, with CID=0, SAC=0, SAM=11, DAC=0 and DAM=11.

For global addresses, the 6LBR MUST include a 6LoWPAN Context Option (6CO) for every prefix it advertises for autoconfiguration. A 6LN then signals the context and fully elides the latest registered source address with CID=1, SAC=1 and SAM=11. The 6LBR can infer it from the assigned prefix and its Neighbor Cache. If the destination also has a context, the 6LN uses CID=1, DAC=1 and DAM=01 or DAM=11. The 6LBR does the mirror image when sending to a 6LN.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides already know who is talking, so they skip writing the full address on every message. It is like writing "me" instead of your whole name.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
DECT ULE secures traffic at the DLC layer with encryption and per-message authentication in CCM mode, similar to RFC 3610, using AES128. Pairing generates a master User Authentication Key (UAK), and session keys are generated during location registration or PVC setup, both using the DSAA2 algorithm. Keys are individual for each FP-PP binding, so PPs share no encryption key.

The RFC still recommends secure transport or application protocols above 6LoWPAN. On privacy, link-local configuration only reveals to the 6LBR what it already knows from the link. For non-link-local addresses a 6LN SHOULD by default use a randomly generated IID or one of the alternative schemes listed earlier. The RFC makes no IANA requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are locked with a key that is different for every gadget, so one gadget cannot read another's mail. It is still smart to add your own lock on top.
